## Observed Facts

- **Data Scope:** BGL, 2005-06-01 to 2005-07-01, no other filters. The dataset starts on 2005-06-03 [E1]. It holds 1,240,932 Log Entries for that window [E2].
- **Busiest day:** 2005-06-14 has 381,561 Log Entries [E2]. The next busiest days are 2005-06-11 with 152,669 and 2005-06-05 with 101,380 [E2].
- **Affected components in June 2005:**
  - KERNEL: 1,219,871 Log Entries [E3]
  - APP: 13,409 [E3]
  - DISCOVERY: 7,290 [E3]
  - LINKCARD: 245 [E3]
  - HARDWARE: 69 [E3]
  - MMCS: 18 [E3]
  - FATAL: 15 [E3]
  - CMCS: 12 [E3]
  - BGLMASTER: 3 [E3]
- KERNEL accounts for almost all of the month's volume. These are counts of Log Entries, not incidents.

## Hypotheses

- The 2005-06-14 spike, and possibly the spikes on 06-11 and 06-05, may be events worth reviewing first. A high Log Entry count alone doesn't show an outage. Repeated messages can inflate it.
- The 15 FATAL and 69 HARDWARE Log Entries are small in number but may point to more serious faults. I haven't examined their content.

## Unknowns

- **Cost:** The logs contain no financial data. I can't say what any June 2005 event cost.
- **Downtime hours and customer impact:** The logs don't record service availability or customer sessions. I can't establish downtime hours or what customers saw. I also haven't found anything that marks a specific "outage" in June 2005. The spikes above are only volume peaks.
- **Which event you mean:** I don't know which event you are calling the outage, or its start and end times.

## Next Step

Look at the 2005-06-14 spike. Break it down by level, node and alert_tag, and read the FATAL and HARDWARE entries around it. That would show whether it was a real fault and which components it involved. Cost and downtime would have to come from incident tickets, billing, or monitoring and SLA records outside these logs.
